title: Home Health Documentation Software: What to Look For in 2026
summary: Cut through the noise on home health documentation tools and find software that actually saves your team time.
body_text: Home health documentation is one of the most time-consuming parts of running an agency. After every call and every in-home assessment, someone on your team has to write it all up: visit notes, care plan updates, follow-up emails, intake records. If that someone is you, you already know how fast an hour disappears. The right home health documentation software can cut that work down dramatically. But the category is crowded, and not every tool is built for the realities of a small or mid-sized agency. This guide breaks down what to actually look for, what to ignore, and how AI is changing what's possible in 2026. If you're still tracking client information in spreadsheets, moving to a structured system for home care operations is the single highest-leverage change you can make this year. Why Documentation Keeps Slipping Through the Cracks Most agency owners don't have a documentation problem because they're disorganized. They have one because documentation happens at the worst possible moment: right after a call or assessment, when you're already behind on the next thing. The result is notes written from memory hours later, care plan drafts that sit unfinished, and follow-up emails that go out a day too late. In a home care business where speed and professionalism win clients, that lag is expensive. Good documentation software doesn't just give you a place to store information. It reduces the effort required to create and maintain that information in the first place. Core Features to Evaluate After every call and assessment, your documentation stack either saves you time or costs you time. Here is what the best tools actually do. Post-Call and Post-Visit Documentation This is the most important capability to evaluate. After a call or in-home assessment, how quickly can your team get accurate, complete documentation into the system? Look for software that: Automatically logs call activity to the right client or lead record Generates draft summaries, follow-up emails, or care plan notes from the conversation Have staff review and approve documentation quickly rather than writing from scratch Stores recordings and transcripts tied to each contact The gap between tools here is significant. Basic software gives you a form to fill out. AI-powered tools generate a first draft for you. That difference can save 15 to 25 minutes per client interaction, which adds up fast across a week of calls and assessments. Care Plan Creation and Updates Care plans sit at the center of your documentation workflow. Every intake conversation, assessment visit, and service change touches the care plan. Software that handles this well should: Support structured care plan templates aligned to common service types Allow updates to be drafted and reviewed without re-entering the same information twice Sync care plan data with your agency management system so records stay consistent If you're using WellSky or AxisCare, bidirectional sync matters a great deal here. Manual re-entry between systems is one of the most common sources of documentation errors. To understand how AI intake software fits into this broader workflow, the complete 2026 guide to AI intake software for home care covers the full picture from first contact to care plan. Record Management and Retrieval Documentation is only useful if people can find it. Evaluate how the software organizes client records and whether your team can pull up a complete history of every call, note, and document for a given client without digging through multiple places. Here are the key questions to ask: Is every interaction (calls, emails, assessments) logged to a single client record automatically? Can you search across client records by name, status, or date? Is the activity history complete enough that a new staff member could get up to speed on a client quickly? What AI Actually Does in Documentation Software AI is showing up in a lot of product marketing right now, so it's worth being specific about what it does and doesn't do in documentation tools. What AI does well: Generating draft summaries from call recordings or assessment notes Suggesting care plan language based on what was discussed Drafting follow-up emails that sound professional and include relevant details Flagging incomplete records or missing information What AI doesn't do: Make clinical decisions or provide medical guidance Replace the judgment of a licensed professional on care needs Guarantee accuracy without human review The best documentation tools using AI technology in home care position it as a drafting assistant, not a replacement for your intake coordinator or care manager. Your staff reviews and approves before anything goes out or gets saved. That human checkpoint is what keeps documentation accurate and keeps your agency protected. Research on what home care consumers actually expect from agencies shows that responsiveness and professionalism are top trust drivers, and well-structured documentation directly supports both. How to Compare Documentation Software: A Practical Checklist What to Evaluate Questions to Ask Post-call automation Does it generate draft notes or emails after calls? Care plan tools Can you create and update plans without double entry? AMS integration Does it sync with WellSky or AxisCare bidirectionally? Communications logging Are calls and assessments automatically tied to records? HIPAA compliance Is the platform fully HIPAA-compliant with BAA available? Ease of use Can a non-technical staff member learn it in a day? Mobile access Does it work on iOS for field-based assessment recording? Pricing model Is it transparent and sized for small agencies? For a broader look at how documentation tools fit into your overall software stack, the non-medical home care software comparison for 2026 is a useful reference point before you make any purchasing decisions. Red Flags to Watch For Not all documentation software is built with small agencies in mind. Watch out for: Overpromising on automation. If a vendor says AI will handle your documentation without human review, that's a risk. Accurate records require a human to confirm the details, especially for care plans and intake notes. No AMS integration. If your documentation tool doesn't connect to your agency management system, you'll be entering the same data in two places. That's not an upgrade. Built for large health systems. Some documentation platforms are designed for hospital networks or large home health companies. The complexity, pricing, and feature set won't match what a small agency actually needs. Vague HIPAA compliance claims. Ask specifically whether the vendor offers a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) and how data is stored and encrypted. Don't accept "we take security seriously" as an answer. How Sage Care Approaches Documentation Sage Care is a HIPAA-compliant client intake automation platform built specifically for home care agencies. After every call or in-home assessment, Sage Care's AI generates summaries, draft follow-up emails, care plan updates, and record suggestions. Your team reviews, edits if needed, and approves with one tap. Work that used to take 15 to 30 minutes now takes under 5. All communications are automatically logged to the right client and contact records. Sage Care also includes bidirectional sync with WellSky and AxisCare, so care plan data stays consistent across your systems without manual re-entry. You can learn more about the Sage Care and WellSky integration and how it fits into a connected home care workflow. Sage Care isn't a clinical tool and it doesn't replace your care team's judgment. It handles the admin layer: the summaries, the follow-ups, the record-keeping, and the care plan drafts that used to eat up your afternoons. Ready to Cut Documentation Time in Half? If your team is spending 20 or 30 minutes writing up every client interaction, Sage Care was built to fix that. See how AI-powered documentation and intake automation works for real agencies. Schedule a demo and try Sage Care free for 30 days. Frequently Asked Questions What is home health documentation software? Home health documentation software helps agencies create, store, and manage client records, care plans, visit notes, and communication history in one place, often with automation to reduce manual data entry. Does documentation software need to be HIPAA-compliant? Yes. Any software that stores or processes protected health information (PHI) for a home care client must be HIPAA-compliant, and the vendor must sign a Business Associate Agreement with your agency. Can AI write care plan notes automatically? AI can generate draft care plan notes based on call recordings or assessment inputs, but a trained staff member should always review and approve them before the notes are finalized or shared.

title: Alight study finds improvements in wellbeing while economic anxieties linger as workers seek more guidance on benefits
summary: The 2025 Alight Employee Mindset Study reveals a paradox: workers feel better overall, yet daily strain, communication overload and rapid change threaten progress to wellbeing – offering key takeaways for employers.
body_text: Facing rapid technological change, economic uncertainty and shifting workplace expectations, employees have remained resilient with reports of feeling better about their wellbeing compared to previous years, according to the 2025 Alight Employee Mindset Study . Nearly half of employees (47%) now rate their overall wellbeing positively—a three-point increase from 2024—with incremental gains in social and mental health. Employee engagement is also trending upwards, with 63% of respondents reporting positive energy and excitement at work and 66% feeling a genuine sense of belonging in their workplace. Even with such progress, challenges remain, as 39% of employees say they dread starting their workday—up five points since 2023—while 34% say they have lost trust in their employer’s wellbeing efforts, a seven-point increase over the same period. “While it’s encouraging to see employees reporting stronger wellbeing, employers can’t afford to lose momentum,” said Laine Thomas Conway, vice president of delivery enablement and engagement at Alight. “Return-to-office tensions, rising burnout and AI uncertainty are adding points of friction to the employee experience. Employees are seeking further guidance from their employers on how to make sense of the resources available to them to improve and maintain their wellbeing. By pairing a high-tech, human-first benefits strategy with flexible work options and clear, personalized communication, employers can turn access into action—driving stronger wellbeing and productivity despite ongoing change." Key insights from the 2025 Employee Mindset Study include : Workers want more than just benefits — they need clear communication and help Availability of employer-sponsored wellbeing programs continue to expand, with 85% of employees reporting access to at least one program, up from 78% in 2022. Yet program utilization remains low, averaging just 30–35%, signaling a need for clearer guidance and practical support from employers. Communication is another area for improvement. While 63% of employees feel more informed about benefits than in previous years, 46% say the volume of communication is overwhelming—an eight-point increase since 2024 — suggesting a need for personalized communication through a combination of technology and human support to be effective. Flexible work environments remain key to employee satisfaction and retention Working arrangements have a clear influence on employee wellbeing. An overwhelming 86% of remote workers are satisfied with where and how they work, the highest percentage among any work arrangement. On the other hand, 40% of hybrid workers report increased feelings of loneliness, compared to 35% of fully remote workers and 26% of those working onsite. However, the key to a successful wellbeing strategy does not necessarily involve return-to-office mandates; choice plays a big part in how workers feel about where they work. While 72% of self-scheduled hybrid workers are happy with their situation, only 53% of company-scheduled hybrid workers feel the same. The good news is that among hybrid employees, 61% report feeling connected to coworkers, compared to 51% of remote workers and 46% of onsite employees, suggesting the need to incorporate flexible working options. Additionally, 35% say they’d be willing to take a pay cut to gain more flexibility in their life. Employees approach AI with both caution and acceptance AI adoption is rising, with one in four employees using AI tools daily. However, attitudes toward AI also strongly correlate with feelings of wellbeing: 56% of employees who feel anxious about AI dread starting their workday, compared with 23% of those unafraid of the technology. AI-worried employees are more likely to feel overwhelmed by benefits choices (25% vs. 8%) and report higher stress (75% vs. 63%). “The findings from this year’s study highlight the critical need for employers to provide their employees with clear direction and expert guidance. By equipping their workforce to navigate rapid disruptions and prioritize their wellbeing, organizations can nurture engagement, boost retention, and avoid the risk of losing valuable talent,” said Rob Austin, vice president of value engineering at Alight. “Embracing flexibility is equally vital as it creates a win-win situation for employers and employees. When employees feel supported, they can put their best foot forward, drive business success and stay committed to their organization.”

title: OGE Energy Corp. reports second quarter 2026 results
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about OGE Energy Corporation's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: OGE Energy Corp. reports second quarter 2026 results July 29, 2026 PDF Version OKLAHOMA CITY , July 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- OGE Energy Corp. (NYSE: OGE), the parent company of Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company ("OG&E"), today reported earnings of $0.56 per diluted share during the three months that ended June 30, 2026, compared to $0.53 per diluted share in the second quarter 2025. OG&E, a regulated electric company, contributed earnings of $0.58 per diluted share in the second quarter, compared to earnings of $0.53 per diluted share in the second quarter 2025. Other operations, which includes the holding company, contributed a loss of $0.02 per diluted share compared to breakeven results in the second quarter of 2025. "Our second-quarter results reflect the strength of our business and the disciplined execution of our team as we advance investments that support reliable, affordable service for customers," said Sean Trauschke, Chairman, President, and CEO of OGE Energy Corp. "We are making significant progress on initiatives that position OG&E for incremental growth while maintaining a strong focus on protecting existing customers as we prepare to serve new large-load opportunities and support economic development." Second Quarter 2026 results OG&E contributed net income of $120.1 million, or $0.58 per diluted share, in the second quarter compared to $107.7 million, or $0.53 per diluted share, in the same period 2025. The increase in net income was primarily due to increased recovery of capital investments and lower interest expense, partially offset by increased operation and maintenance expenses. Other Operations resulted in a loss of $3.8 million, or $0.02 per diluted share, in the second quarter compared to a loss of $0.2 million, in the same period 2025. The increased loss was primarily due to higher interest expense and a one-time benefit related to legacy midstream operations recognized in 2025, which was partially offset by increased other income. OGE Energy's net income was $116.3 million or $0.56 per diluted share in the second quarter, compared to earnings of $107.5 million, or $0.53 per diluted share, in the same period 2025. 2026 Outlook OGE Energy's 2026 consolidated earnings guidance remains unchanged and is projected to be $2.43 per average diluted share, within a range of $2.38 to $2.48 per average diluted share. The guidance assumes, among other things, normal weather for the remainder of the year. OG&E has significant seasonality in its earnings due to weather on a year-over-year basis. See OGE Energy's 2025 Form 10-K for other key factors and assumptions underlying its 2026 guidance. Conference Call Webcast OGE Energy Corp. will host an earnings and business update conference call on Wednesday, July 29, 2026, at 8 a.m. CDT. The conference will be available through the Investor Center at www.oge.com . What Is a Home Health Aide & What Do They Do?
summary: We over everything you need to know about a career as a home health aide: what they do each day, where they work, how much they make, and how to become one.
body_text: A home health aide, or HHA, is a trained caregiver who helps people with daily activities and basic health needs at home. The work home health aides do makes a world of difference for millions of older adults, people with disabilities, and those recovering from illness or surgery. That may be why it’s one of the fastest-growing jobs in the country. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) projects a 17% job growth rate for home health and personal care aides in the next decade. That’s much higher than the 3% average growth they expect for other occupations. The role is also flexible. HHAs can choose to work full-time or part-time, with one long-term client or several, and in private homes or in more formal settings like assisted living communities. HHA training can take just a few weeks, and all you need is a high school diploma or GED to get started. This guide will tell you everything you need to know about a career as a home health aide. We’ll cover what they do each day, where they work, how much they make, and the steps you need to take to become one. Before diving in, here's a summary of the home health aide career: At a Glance Home Health Aide (HHA) 🛁 Core Duties Personal care (bathing, dressing, mobility), basic health monitoring (vitals, medication reminders), and household support (light housekeeping, companionship) 🏠 Where They Work Mostly private homes, plus assisted living communities, group homes, and day services programs 🎓 Education Needed High school diploma or GED (some states allow exceptions); no college required 📋 Training Time A few weeks to a few months; federal minimum of 75 hours (16 classroom + 16 hands-on) ✅ Certification Pass a competency evaluation; many states also require a certification exam and registry listing 💰 Average Salary $36,120/year, or $17.36/hour 📈 Top Earners $45,040/year, or $21.65/hour (top 10%) 🚀 Job Growth 17% projected growth over the next decade — much faster than the 3% average for all jobs 🤝 Key Skills Compassion, attention to detail, communication, physical stamina, patience, reliability What Is a Home Health Aide? A home health aide is a trained caregiver who helps people with daily tasks they cannot do safely on their own. This includes bathing, moving around the house, and monitoring basic health signs. Most of their clients are older adults, people with chronic illnesses or disabilities, or people recovering after a hospital stay or surgery. The main goal is to help them stay safe and comfortable at home, so they do not have to move into a hospital or skilled nursing facility. HHAs work under the supervision of a registered nurse or other licensed healthcare professional. They follow a written care plan , created by the patient’s providers, that details the services they need, how often they need them, and their goals. However, HHAs mostly work without a supervisor present, so they need good judgment and a strong sense of responsibility, along with clinical skills. Sometimes, home health aides and personal care aides get confused. The BLS tracks them in the same category. Personal care aides are also professional caregivers, but they are limited to providing nonmedical services . Their work focuses on companionship and daily living tasks like cooking and transportation. They typically make a little less money than HHAs, and their clients are more often people with developmental or intellectual disabilities. Because HHAs do more clinical tasks and hands-on patient care, they often use their experience as a stepping stone to higher-paying clinical jobs like medical assistant. What a home health aide does every day mostly depends on the care plan of their client and the rules of their state or the agency they work for. Most days involve a combination of personal care, health monitoring, and household help. Personal Care Duties These may include: Assisting with bathing, dressing, and grooming so clients feel clean and comfortable Helping clients move safely, including transfers between a bed and a chair and the use of walkers or wheelchairs Assisting with toileting and incontinence care Preparing meals and helping with feeding when needed, including following any special diets Health-Related Duties Depending on the state and the client's care plan, HHAs may also do some basic health monitoring tasks, such as: Checking and recording vital signs, like blood pressure, pulse, and temperature Reminding clients to take medication, and in some cases helping with medication a client would normally take on their own Watching for changes in a client's condition and reporting them to the supervising provider Different states have different rules about what HHAs can do, especially when it comes to medications. The ability to give insulin injections, for example, varies widely by state. New York created a special Advanced Home Health Aide (AHHA) certification that allows specially trained aides to give insulin injections under nurse supervision. Texas , Washington , Minnesota , and Wisconsin allow a nurse to delegate insulin administration to a trained aide, though usually only in certain settings, like assisted living, or for a specific client. Florida is often mischaracterized as banning aides from giving any medication, but its rule actually carves out an exception for prefilled insulin syringes and epi-pens. Most states, like California , just don’t allow it. Household and Companionship Duties These may include: Light housekeeping, laundry, and errands Grocery shopping and meal planning Providing companionship and conversation, which can be very important for clients who live alone Accompanying clients to medical appointments and outings Helping organize a client's schedule and keeping notes for family members or the care team What a Home Health Aide Cannot Do Federal rules spell out clear limits on what a home health aide can do. Under federal regulations , an HHA's tasks must be ordered by a physician, included in the client's care plan, allowed under state law, and consistent with the aide's training. Generally, HHAs cannot: Diagnose conditions Write a care plan Give injections Provide sterile wound care Some tasks that seem simple, like helping patients with medications they would normally take on their own, require extra certification in many states. You can usually find details about scope of practice for HHAs from your state’s nursing board . Where Do Home Health Aides Work? The majority of HHAs work with individuals in their homes. BLS data says 49% of HHAs and personal care aides provide individual and family services, and an additional 24% provide home healthcare services. Here are some of the settings where HHAs work: Private homes: This is the most common workplace for HHAs. Aides may work with one client long-term or rotate between several. Schedules can range from a few hours a week to live-in care. Assisted living and continuing care communities: These settings provide care primarily for older people. HHAs may help several different residents with daily tasks in a single shift. Group homes and residential facilities: These locations serve people with intellectual or developmental disabilities. Day services programs: These settings provide support and supervision for clients during daytime hours, often so family caregivers can work or rest. Skills and Qualities of a Successful Home Health Aide Professional caregiving requires technical, physical, and interpersonal skills in equal amounts. Here are some of the qualities that make a great home health aide: Compassion: Clients are facing pain, fear, and loss of independence, so a caring presence is just as important as being technically skilled. Attention to detail: Following care instructions exactly, from wound care steps to medication reminders, keeps clients safe. Integrity: Clients and families need to trust an aide who is often alone with them in their home. Communication skills: Aides need to listen closely and report changes clearly to a supervising nurse or case manager. Physical stamina: The role can involve lifting, standing, and helping clients move for much of a shift. Patience: Progress may be slow, especially for clients with chronic conditions or memory loss, so calm and patience are critical for success. Reliability: Clients rely on aides to arrive on time because missing a visit can mean missing meals or medications. Home Health Aide Requirements and Certification Requirements vary by state and employer. However, the federal government has created standards for home health and hospice agencies that get Medicare or Medicaid funding. This gives a baseline that most states and agencies use, though they may add additional requirements on top of it. Training Requirements Most training programs require candidates to be at least 18 years old, though some states allow younger applicants. A high school diploma or equivalent is commonly required, but not in every case. Federal rules require agencies certified by Medicare or Medicaid to employ HHAs who have had at least 75 hours of training, including a minimum of 16 hours of classroom instruction followed by at least 16 hours of supervised, hands-on practice. After training, aides must pass a competency evaluation. Many states also require a separate state certification exam. Many employers require a background check and current CPR and first aid certification before an aide can start working with clients. Federal vs. State Requirements The federal training minimum only applies to HHAs working for agencies certified by Medicare or Medicaid. States and individual employers are free to require more, whether that's additional training hours, a separate exam, or listing on a state aide registry. This is why two aides trained in different states can have different credentials, even if they have the same job title. It’s a good idea to check your state's requirements before starting a training program. Home Health Aide Salary and Job Outlook The best thing about starting a career as a home health aide is how strong the demand is for workers. The population of the U.S. is aging, and more people prefer to live in home and community-based settings now than ever before. This shift is creating many new jobs for home health workers. It is also a job that cannot be automated or sent offshore. The BLS combines home health and personal care aides into one category. For that category, it reported that there were over 4.3 million jobs in 2025 . The BLS also estimates that job openings will continue to grow. It projects a 17% job growth rate for these occupations in the next decade, much faster than the 3% average for all jobs. That’s about 765,800 job openings each year, on average, over the decade. How much HHAs make depends on geographical location, experience level, employer type (agency vs. private), and any special certifications they may have. The average wage for home health and personal care aides is $36,120 per year or $17.36 per hour . The top 10% in the field make an average of $45,040 per year, or $21.65 per hour. The BLS lists the states with the highest annual wage as Washington, Oregon, Rhode Island, DC, and Vermont. Another positive aspect of this role is the opportunity for career growth. The patient care experience and interpersonal skills you build as an HHA transfer directly up the career ladder. Many HHAs continue their training to move onto more advanced medical roles . Here at Stepful, we have training for caregivers designed exactly for this. HHAs often go on to become medical assistants , nursing assistants, or a nurse (LPN or RN). Home Health Aide FAQs Does Medicare cover a home health aide? Medicare covers part-time or intermittent home health services only if the patient is considered homebound and a healthcare provider orders the care. It must be provided by a Medicare-certified home health agency. Medicare does not cover help with daily tasks like bathing or dressing unless it is deemed medically necessary and the patient is also getting skilled nursing care. How much does it cost to hire a home health aide? Private-pay, in-home, non-medical caregiving has a national median rate of about $35 an hour, according to the 2025 CareScout Cost of Care Survey . Rates vary by state and may be lower if paid through Medicaid or a long-term care insurance policy. Can a home health aide give insulin? It depends on the state. Most states do not allow HHAs to give any kind of injection. Some states, like New York , allow specially certified "advanced" aides to do it. Others, like Texas and Washington , allow nurses to delegate the task to trained HHAs. Florida makes an exception for insulin in pre-filled syringes. Can a CNA work as a home health aide? Yes. Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs) usually complete more training and are allowed to do more for patients than HHAs, so they can easily work as HHAs. HHAs, however, would need more training hours and a state competency exam before they could work as CNAs. Learn more about a career as a home health aide vs. certified nursing assistant here . Do I need a license to become a home health aide? Most states require certification instead of a traditional professional license. This usually means completing an approved training program and passing a certification exam. Some states then keep a registry of certified HHAs. The steps and paperwork vary by state, so check with your state's health department before you begin. How long does it take to become a home health aide? Training can take a few weeks to a few months, depending on your state and the program. The federal minimum for agencies certified by Medicare or Medicaid is 75 hours of classroom and supervised practical training. Some states require more hours or an extra exam, which can add time. Is a home health aide the same as a caregiver? Caregiver is a broad, informal term for anyone providing care, including unpaid family members and professional, paid healthcare workers. A home health aide is a trained, often certified, professional with specific duties who usually works for an employer or agency. Is being a home health aide hard? Being an HHA can be physically and emotionally demanding. It involves lifting, long hours on your feet, and helping people through tough health changes. It may also require working evenings, weekends, or holidays at times. However, many HHAs say the relationships they build with clients make the hard work worth it. Can home health aides work in hospitals? Not usually. Home health aide services are defined by Medicare as taking place at a patient's residence, which specifically excludes hospitals and skilled nursing facilities. HHAs mainly work in private homes, assisted living communities, group homes, and hospice settings, while hospitals use nursing assistants and orderlies for similar support. If you are interested in working in a hospital, explore becoming a patient care technician or medical assistant . What's the difference between a home health aide and a personal care aide? The terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but they are different roles . HHAs usually get more training and can do basic health monitoring tasks. Personal care aides are limited to providing nonmedical services . Their work focuses on companionship and daily living tasks like cooking and transportation. Personal care aides typically make less money than HHAs, and their clients are more often people with developmental or intellectual disabilities.
